name: Mary Wollstonecraft
description: British writer who defended women’s education and challenged hereditary political and social privilege.
scope: Public positions and conduct during the specified period; this represents the individual rather than all party members or citizens.

axes.brief: Republican representation and criticism of hereditary authority favoured accountable government.
axes.counter: Exact universal suffrage and modern judicial design remain reconstructed responses.

axes.brief: Reason, civil liberty and criticism of arbitrary authority favoured personal independence.
axes.counter: Moral duties and modesty do not automatically imply legal prohibition.

axes.brief: Universal reason and criticism of inherited prejudice support cultural equality.
axes.counter: National education and contemporary European assumptions qualify modern accommodation analogies.

axes.brief: Universal rights and cosmopolitan revolutionary sympathies supply open-movement context.
axes.counter: No detailed modern numerical, asylum or welfare admissions scheme was established.

axes.brief: Criticism of standing military hierarchies and arbitrary power favoured peaceful civic life.
axes.counter: Support for revolutionary reform does not entail pacifism at all costs.

axes.brief: Universal human rights and republican solidarity crossed borders.
axes.counter: This is distinct from approval of every contemporary supranational institution.

axes.brief: Criticism of unequal property and support for public education limited exclusive private provision.
axes.counter: She did not articulate modern nationalisation across all industries.

axes.brief: Criticism of aristocratic privilege and commercial dependence supplies tentative open-trade context.
axes.counter: Specific modern tariffs and strategic investment rules remain undocumented.

axes.brief: Independent livelihoods coexisted with national educational responsibilities.
axes.counter: No modern comprehensive economic production plan was established.

axes.brief: Economic independence and criticism of great inequality support social opportunity.
axes.counter: Modern progressive taxes and compensated land redistribution are analogical estimates.

axes.brief: Religious moral reasoning coexisted with criticism of ecclesiastical and inherited authority.
axes.counter: Belief in God does not establish clerical approval of civil policy.

axes.brief: Women’s education and equal rational capacity challenged prescribed dependency.
axes.counter: Modesty, maternal duties and sexual virtue limit automatic attribution of contemporary sexual liberalism.

axes.brief: Educational improvement and reason favoured beneficial development.
axes.counter: Modern technology risk thresholds have no direct counterpart.

axes.brief: National education coexisted with republican accountability and local participation.
axes.counter: Modern federal and Indigenous jurisdiction questions are especially remote analogies.

axes.brief: Gendered education and dependence, rather than inferior rational nature, explained women’s apparent disadvantages.
axes.counter: Reason’s universality does not establish that every temperamental trait is solely social.
